THE "PRIMARILY ENGAGED IN" DUTIES TEST FOR THE EXECUTIVE, ADMINISTRATIVE, AND PROFESSIONAL EXEMPTIONS (LAB. CODE § 515; WAGE ORDER 4-2001, § 1(A); RAMIREZ V. YOSEMITE WATER; HEYEN V. SAFEWAY) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

PURPOSE AND SCOPE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Acme, Inc. maintains this information sheet to describe what California law says about the "primarily engaged in" duties test that governs the executive, administrative, and professional overtime exemptions — the test that applies to a position such as Assistant Store Manager, held by Jordan Lee. This document describes the overtime requirement the exemptions operate against, the statutory framework in Labor Code section 515, the quantitative more-than-one-half-of-work-time definition of "primarily" in section 515(e) and in the Industrial Welfare Commission wage orders, the duties tests for each of the three exemptions as stated in Wage Order 4-2001, the salary component, the difference between California’s quantitative test and the federal "primary duty" test (Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co.), how time spent doing exempt and nonexempt tasks at the same time is treated (Heyen v. Safeway Inc.), the "realistic requirements of the job" rule, the treatment of working supervisors, who bears the burden of proof, and what the exemptions do not reach. It describes the law; it does not classify any employee as exempt or nonexempt and does not evaluate any particular job.

THE OVERTIME REQUIREMENT AND THE STATUTORY FRAME OF THE THREE EXEMPTIONS
California law requires overtime compensation for work beyond eight hours in a workday and beyond 40 hours in a workweek, and for the first eight hours worked on the seventh day of work in a workweek, at no less than one and one-half times the regular rate of pay, with a double-time requirement for work beyond 12 hours in a day and beyond eight hours on a seventh day (Labor Code section 510(a)).

Labor Code section 515(a) is the statute that permits the Industrial Welfare Commission to establish exemptions from that requirement for executive, administrative, and professional employees. By its terms the section permits those exemptions only where three things are true of the employee: the employee is primarily engaged in the duties that meet the test of the exemption; the employee customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties; and the employee earns a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment. Section 515(c) defines "full-time employment" for that purpose as employment in which an employee is employed for 40 hours per week, and section 515(e) defines "primarily" for purposes of the section as more than one-half of the employee’s worktime.

THE WAGE ORDER’S "PRIMARILY ENGAGED IN" REQUIREMENT AND ITS MORE-THAN-HALF DEFINITION
Section 1(A) of Wage Order 4-2001 provides that Sections 3 through 12 of the order — the sections containing the hours, overtime, minimum wage, reporting time, records, meal period, and rest period requirements — do not apply to persons employed in administrative, executive, or professional capacities, and that the requirements stated in section 1(A) apply in determining whether an employee’s duties meet the test to qualify for such an exemption.

Each of the three tests requires that the employee be "primarily engaged in" duties that meet the test of the exemption. Section 2(N) of the same order defines "primarily," as that word is used in Section 1, to mean more than one-half the employee’s work time. The wage order also states, in the same subparagraph that imposes the "primarily engaged in" requirement, that the activities constituting exempt and non-exempt work are to be construed in the same manner as they are construed under listed Fair Labor Standards Act regulations in effect as of the date of the order, that exempt work includes work directly and closely related to exempt work, and that the work actually performed during the workweek must first and foremost be examined, together with the employer’s realistic expectations and the realistic requirements of the job.

THE EXECUTIVE EXEMPTION’S DUTIES TEST
Under section 1(A)(1) of Wage Order 4-2001, a person employed in an executive capacity means an employee whose duties and responsibilities involve the management of the enterprise in which the employee is employed or of a customarily recognized department or subdivision of it; who customarily and regularly directs the work of two or more other employees in that unit; who has the authority to hire or fire other employees, or whose suggestions and recommendations as to hiring, firing, advancement, promotion, or other change of status of other employees will be given particular weight; who customarily and regularly exercises discretion and independent judgment; and who is primarily engaged in duties that meet the test of the exemption. The wage order joins these subparagraphs with "and," so each is a separate requirement. A separate subparagraph adds the salary requirement described in a later clause of this document.

THE ADMINISTRATIVE EXEMPTION’S DUTIES TEST
Under section 1(A)(2) of Wage Order 4-2001, a person employed in an administrative capacity means an employee whose duties and responsibilities involve either the performance of office or non-manual work directly related to management policies or general business operations of the employer or the employer’s customers, or the performance of functions in the administration of a school system or educational establishment or institution, or of a department or subdivision of one, in work directly related to the academic instruction or training carried on there. The employee must also customarily and regularly exercise discretion and independent judgment; must regularly and directly assist a proprietor or a bona fide executive or administrative employee, or perform work along specialized or technical lines requiring special training, experience, or knowledge under only general supervision, or execute special assignments and tasks under only general supervision; and must be primarily engaged in duties that meet the test of the exemption. A separate subparagraph adds the salary requirement described in a later clause of this document.

THE PROFESSIONAL EXEMPTION’S DUTIES TEST
Under section 1(A)(3) of Wage Order 4-2001, a person employed in a professional capacity means an employee who meets all of the listed requirements: the employee is either licensed or certified by the State of California and primarily engaged in the practice of one of eight enumerated recognized professions — law, medicine, dentistry, optometry, architecture, engineering, teaching, or accounting — or is primarily engaged in an occupation commonly recognized as a learned or artistic profession, which the order defines by reference to advanced knowledge acquired by prolonged specialized intellectual instruction or to original and creative work in a recognized field of artistic endeavor. The employee must customarily and regularly exercise discretion and independent judgment in performing those duties, and must earn the monthly salary described in a later clause of this document. Unlike the executive and administrative tests, the professional test states the "primarily engaged" requirement inside the description of the qualifying practice or occupation itself.

THE SALARY COMPONENT THAT ACCOMPANIES EACH DUTIES TEST
Each of the three exemptions carries a salary requirement in addition to its duties test. Wage Order 4-2001 states, for the executive and administrative exemptions, that such an employee must also earn a monthly salary equivalent to no less than two times the state minimum wage for full-time employment, and that full-time employment is defined in Labor Code section 515(c) as 40 hours per week; the professional exemption states the same requirement in its own subparagraph. Because the threshold is expressed as a multiple of the state minimum wage, it moves whenever the minimum wage does. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states that, effective January 1, 2026, the California minimum wage is $16.90 per hour for all employers not otherwise covered by a higher industry-specific or local minimum wage. Two times that hourly rate is $33.80; at 40 hours per week that is $1,352 per week, which corresponds to a monthly salary of about $5,858.67 and an annual salary of $70,304. Meeting the salary figure does not by itself make a position exempt: the wage order states the salary requirement in addition to, not instead of, the duties requirements.

CALIFORNIA’S QUANTITATIVE TEST COMPARED WITH THE FEDERAL "PRIMARY DUTY" TEST
The California and federal tests are built differently. Under the federal Fair Labor Standards Act regulations, an employee whose "primary duty" is exempt work is exempt regardless of how much of the employee’s time that duty actually occupies. California instead asks how the employee’s work time was actually spent. In Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., the California Supreme Court described the state’s approach to the outside salesperson exemption as "a purely quantitative approach" that differs from the qualitative federal method, and observed in a footnote that the same distinction runs through the exemption for administrative, executive, and professional employees: the federal test turns on the employee’s "primary duty," while the state exemption requires that the employee be "engaged . . . primarily" in exempt work, with "primarily" defined as more than one-half the employee’s work time. The Division of Labor Standards Enforcement’s Enforcement Manual states the same comparison as its enforcement position and records that the Industrial Welfare Commission described its "quantitative test" as more protective of employees than the federal "qualitative" or "primary duty" test.

TIME SPENT DOING EXEMPT AND NONEXEMPT WORK AT THE SAME TIME
A recurring question is how to count time during which an employee performs exempt and nonexempt tasks simultaneously — a store manager who supervises while bagging groceries, for example. In Heyen v. Safeway Inc., the employer argued that all such hours should be counted as exempt, as they would be under the current federal regulation on concurrent duties. The Court of Appeal rejected that argument as inconsistent with California law and affirmed a judgment for the employee. Reading the 2001 federal regulations that Wage Order 7 incorporates, the court concluded that those regulations recognize no "hybrid" category and instead require each discrete task to be classified as either exempt or nonexempt, and that identical tasks may fall on either side depending on the purpose they serve — a task done because it is helpful in supervising employees or contributes to the smooth functioning of the department is exempt, while the same task done for a different, nonmanagerial reason is not. The court noted that although the federal regulations adopted by the Secretary of Labor in 2004 say that concurrent performance of exempt and nonexempt work does not disqualify an employee from the executive exemption, in the nine years since then neither the California Legislature nor the Industrial Welfare Commission had elected to follow them, so the court had no authority to do so.

THE "REALISTIC REQUIREMENTS OF THE JOB" RULE
The wage order directs that the work actually performed during the workweek be examined first and foremost, together with the employer’s realistic expectations and the realistic requirements of the job. That phrasing comes from Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., where the California Supreme Court explained that neither an employer’s job description nor the employee’s own choices can be the sole measure: if hours were counted according to the employer’s job description, an employer could make an employee exempt merely by writing an idealized description with little basis in reality, while an employee who falls below the halfway mark through his or her own substandard performance should not thereby escape a valid exemption. The court directed that a trial court consider, first and foremost, how the employee actually spends his or her time, and also whether the employee’s practice diverges from the employer’s realistic expectations, whether there was any concrete expression of employer displeasure over substandard performance, and whether those expressions were themselves realistic given the actual overall requirements of the job. Heyen v. Safeway applied that rule to the executive exemption, and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states the same rule as its enforcement position.

expectedJSON.body: A recurring question is how to count time during which an employee performs exempt and nonexempt tasks simultaneously — a store manager who supervises while bagging groceries, for example. In Heyen v. Safeway Inc., the employer argued that all such hours should be counted as exempt, as they would be under the current federal regulation on concurrent duties. The Court of Appeal rejected that argument as inconsistent with California law and affirmed a judgment for the employee. Reading the 2001 federal regulations that Wage Order 7 incorporates, the court concluded that those regulations recognize no "hybrid" category and instead require each discrete task to be classified as either exempt or nonexempt, and that identical tasks may fall on either side depending on the purpose they serve — a task done because it is helpful in supervising employees or contributes to the smooth functioning of the department is exempt, while the same task done for a different, nonmanagerial reason is not. The court noted that although the federal regulations adopted by the Secretary of Labor in 2004 say that concurrent performance of exempt and nonexempt work does not disqualify an employee from the executive exemption, in the nine years since then neither the California Legislature nor the Industrial Welfare Commission had elected to follow them, so the court had no authority to do so.

expectedJSON.body: The wage order directs that the work actually performed during the workweek be examined first and foremost, together with the employer’s realistic expectations and the realistic requirements of the job. That phrasing comes from Ramirez v. Yosemite Water Co., where the California Supreme Court explained that neither an employer’s job description nor the employee’s own choices can be the sole measure: if hours were counted according to the employer’s job description, an employer could make an employee exempt merely by writing an idealized description with little basis in reality, while an employee who falls below the halfway mark through his or her own substandard performance should not thereby escape a valid exemption. The court directed that a trial court consider, first and foremost, how the employee actually spends his or her time, and also whether the employee’s practice diverges from the employer’s realistic expectations, whether there was any concrete expression of employer displeasure over substandard performance, and whether those expressions were themselves realistic given the actual overall requirements of the job. Heyen v. Safeway applied that rule to the executive exemption, and the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement states the same rule as its enforcement position.

Safeway summarized them, work of the same kind performed by a supervisor’s nonexempt employees is generally nonexempt even when the supervisor performs it, and if such work takes up a large part of a supervisor’s time the supervisor is likely a nonexempt employee. The 2001 version of 29 C.F.R. section 541.115, quoted in that opinion, states that work of the same nature as that performed by subordinates must be counted as nonexempt work and that the exemption does not apply if the amount of such work is substantial. expectedJSON.body: Two general rules govern how the exemptions are applied. First, under California law exemptions from statutory mandatory overtime provisions are narrowly construed. Second, the assertion of an exemption from the overtime laws is an affirmative defense, so the employer bears the burden of proving the employee’s exemption. Because the test is quantitative and the burden is the employer’s, a job title or a written job description does not by itself establish exempt status. In Heyen v. Safeway the Court of Appeal approved a trial court instruction stating that the test of whether the defendants had met their burden to show that the plaintiff spent more than 50 percent of her time engaged in exempt tasks is quantitative, that the fact finder must look first and foremost to the actual tasks performed, and that merely having the duty of managing is not sufficient to establish exempt status.
